| [ARG-117](../../../record/arguments.d/ARG-117.md) | Locke's Second Treatise carries the form of the claim that no delegation can confer what the delegator lacks, but grounds it in the absence of power over one's own life and admits forfeiture by fault, so it does not carry inalienable standing in general | The support judgement the readings of 2026-11-18 make about [CLAIM-720](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-720.md), filed "after Locke's Second Treatise §§22–23 and 135". He does not carry the claim's generality. His ground is that persons are God's "property, whose workmanship they are" (§6), so what cannot be conferred is arbitrary power over life. And he admits forfeiture: one "having by his fault forfeited his own life" (§23). The claim lists no wrongdoing among what cannot remove standing, and its defeat condition does not address forfeiture. Proposed: the verdict is the assistant's (Claude, in this session); adopting it is the owner's call. | Proposed |
